বমিভাব, পেটে অস্বস্তি, মুখে ধাতব স্বাদ।
খালি পেটে বমিভাব হলে খাবারের পরে খান।
iron: চা, দুধ ও ক্যালসিয়ামের সাথে নয়; শিশুদের নাগালের বাইরে রাখুন।
folic: গর্ভাবস্থায় শিশুর স্নায়ুনালীর ত্রুটি প্রতিরোধ, ফোলেট-ঘাটতির রক্তস্বল্পতা।
নতুন কোষ ও রক্ত তৈরিতে লাগে।
গর্ভধারণের পরিকল্পনা থেকেই খাওয়া উপকারী; B12 ঘাটতি থাকলে আগে তা পরীক্ষা করুন।
multivitamin: খাদ্যে ভিটামিন-খনিজের ঘাটতি পূরণ, অসুস্থতার পর দুর্বলতা।
বিভিন্ন ভিটামিন ও খনিজ একসাথে সরবরাহ করে।
সুষম খাবারের বিকল্প নয়; একাধিক সাপ্লিমেন্ট একসাথে নিলে মাত্রা বেশি হতে পারে।
glucosamine: তরুণাস্থির (কার্টিলেজ) উপাদান সরবরাহ করে বলে ধারণা করা হয়।
শামুক-চিংড়িতে অ্যালার্জি থাকলে লেবেল দেখুন; ফল পেতে কয়েক সপ্তাহ লাগে।
coq10: হৃদরোগ ও স্ট্যাটিন-জনিত পেশিব্যথায় সহায়ক সাপ্লিমেন্ট হিসেবে।
রক্ত পাতলা করার ওষুধের কার্যকারিতা বদলাতে পারে।
povidone: ক্ষত পরিষ্কার, অপারেশনের আগে চামড়া জীবাণুমুক্ত করা, মাউথওয়াশ।
গিলবেন না; বড় পোড়া বা গভীর ক্ষতে দীর্ঘদিন নয়।
lidocaine: ছোট অপারেশন, দাঁতের চিকিৎসা, ব্যথাযুক্ত জায়গা অবশ করা (জেল/স্প্রে)।
স্নায়ুর ব্যথার সংকেত সাময়িকভাবে বন্ধ করে।
বেশি পরিমাণে বা ভাঙা চামড়ায় বড় জায়গায় নয়।
oxymetazoline: নাকের রক্তনালী সংকুচিত করে ফোলা কমায়।
টানা ৫–৭ দিনের বেশি নয়, নইলে নাক আরও বন্ধ হয়।
timolol: চোখের তরল তৈরি কমায় বা নিষ্কাশন বাড়ায়।
টিমোলল হাঁপানি ও ধীর হৃৎস্পন্দনে সাবধান।
menthol: পেশি ও জোড়ার ব্যথার মলম; স্যালিসাইলিক এসিড খুশকি, ব্রণ ও মোটা চামড়ায়।
চামড়ায় ঠান্ডা-গরম অনুভূতি দিয়ে ব্যথা ঢেকে দেয় বা মৃত চামড়া তোলে।
dextrose: পানিশূন্যতা, শর্করা ও লবণের ঘাটতি পূরণ, শিরায় ওষুধ দেওয়া।
শরীরে পানি, লবণ ও শক্তি সরবরাহ করে।
ors: ডায়রিয়া, বমি, কলেরা ও গরমে পানিশূন্যতায় পানি ও লবণের ঘাটতি পূরণ।
লবণ ও গ্লুকোজ একসাথে অন্ত্র থেকে পানি শোষণ বাড়ায়।
সঠিকভাবে বানালে সাধারণত নিরাপদ; কখনো বমি হতে পারে।
প্যাকেটের নির্দেশমতো নির্দিষ্ট পরিমাণ বিশুদ্ধ পানিতে গুলুন, কম-বেশি নয়। বানানো স্যালাইন ১২ ঘণ্টা পর ফেলে দিন। পানিশূন্যতা বাড়লে, রক্ত-পায়খানা বা শিশু নেতিয়ে পড়লে দ্রুত হাসপাতালে নিন।
erythropoietin: হিমোগ্লোবিন ও রক্তচাপ নিয়মিত পরীক্ষা করতে হয়।
resmetirom: লিভারে চর্বি জমা ও প্রদাহ (MASH/NASH), নির্দিষ্ট রোগীদের ক্ষেত্রে।
লিভারে থাইরয়েড-হরমোন রিসেপ্টরে কাজ করে চর্বি কমায়।

paracetamol: Fever, headache, toothache, body ache and mild to moderate pain.
Reduces prostaglandins in the brain that signal pain and fever.
Generally safe at correct doses; occasionally nausea or skin rash.
Overdose can cause severe liver damage. Never exceed the daily maximum or combine with other paracetamol-containing products.
caffeine: Added to painkillers to improve relief of headache and migraine.
Narrows brain blood vessels and speeds absorption of the painkiller.
Avoid at night or with lots of tea/coffee.
aspirin: Low dose prevents heart attack and stroke; higher dose for pain and fever.
Stops platelets clumping and reduces inflammation.
Not without medical advice in peptic ulcer, bleeding disorders or under 16 years.
ibuprofen: Pain, fever, toothache, period pain and inflammation.
Blocks COX enzymes that cause inflammation.
Do not take on an empty stomach. Avoid in ulcer, kidney disease, heart disease and late pregnancy.
diclofenac: Arthritis, joint and muscle pain, sprains, post-operative pain.
Blocks COX enzymes to reduce pain and swelling.
Long-term use raises risk of ulcer, kidney and heart problems. Take after food.
aceclofenac: Osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, back and joint pain.
Reduces COX enzymes to lower inflammation and pain.
Tell your doctor about ulcer, kidney or heart disease. Take after food.
naproxen: Arthritis, joint pain, period pain, muscle and tendon inflammation.
Blocks COX enzymes to reduce inflammation.
Caution in ulcer, kidney and heart disease; usually taken with food.
ketorolac: Short-term relief of post-operative or severe pain; eye drops for eye inflammation.
Blocks COX enzymes for fast pain relief.
Usually not more than 5 days. Risk of stomach bleeding and kidney damage.
etoricoxib: Osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, gout, dental surgery pain.
Blocks only the inflammatory COX-2 enzyme, with less stomach harm.
Ankle swelling, raised blood pressure, indigestion, headache.
Not suitable in uncontrolled high blood pressure or heart disease.
nabumetone: Pain and swelling of osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis.
Caution in ulcer and kidney disease.
tramadol: Acts on opioid receptors in the brain to reduce pain signals.
Can be habit-forming. Avoid with seizure history or alcohol; prescription only.
pregabalin: Diabetic nerve pain, fibromyalgia; add-on for seizures and anxiety.
Drowsiness, dizziness, weight gain, blurred vision.
Do not stop suddenly. Avoid driving and alcohol.
mirogabalin: Diabetic nerve pain and post-herpetic nerve pain.
Acts on nerve calcium channels to reduce pain signals.
Dose adjusted in kidney disease; do not stop suddenly.
baclofen: Muscle stiffness and spasms from nerve disorders (spasticity).
Acts on the spinal cord to reduce muscle tone.
Stopping suddenly can cause seizures or hallucinations.
tiemonium: Cramping abdominal pain, gallstone and kidney stone colic, period pain.
Relaxes smooth muscle of the gut and urinary tract.
Dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, difficulty passing urine.
Caution in glaucoma and enlarged prostate.
omeprazole: Gastric acidity, heartburn, acid reflux, peptic ulcer, H. pylori treatment.
Headache, stomach pain, diarrhoea or constipation.
Usually 30 minutes before meals. Ask your doctor before long-term use.
esomeprazole: Acidity, acid reflux (GERD), peptic ulcer, prevention of NSAID ulcers.
Take before meals. Long-term use may lower vitamin B12 and magnesium and affect bones.
pantoprazole: Acidity, heartburn, acid reflux and ulcer.
Take before meals; ask your doctor before long-term use.
rabeprazole: Acid reflux, peptic ulcer, H. pylori treatment.
Ask your doctor before long-term use.
dexlansoprazole: Lowers stomach acid for a long period.
Ask your doctor before long-term use.
vonoprazan: Acid reflux, ulcer and H. pylori treatment.
Quickly and strongly blocks the stomach acid pump.
May interact with other medicines; tell your doctor.
famotidine: Blocks the histamine signal for acid production.
Lower dose may be needed in kidney disease.
antacid: Neutralises stomach acid or breaks gas bubbles.
Take 2 hours apart from other medicines; caution in kidney disease.
domperidone: Helps the stomach empty faster and reduces vomiting signals.
Not in heart rhythm problems; usually not longer than 1 week.
ondansetron: Prevents vomiting from chemotherapy, surgery and severe nausea.
Blocks serotonin (5-HT3) receptors in brain and gut.
palonosetron: Prevents vomiting after chemotherapy and surgery.
picosulfate: Constipation and bowel cleansing before colonoscopy.
Increases movement of the large bowel.
Do not use regularly for long; drink plenty of water.
lactulose: Draws water into the bowel to soften stools.
Not for patients needing a galactose-free diet.
ursodeoxycholic: Dissolving small cholesterol gallstones and some liver diseases.
Lowers cholesterol in bile and improves bile flow.
Not when the bile duct is blocked.
nitazoxanide: Diarrhoea caused by Giardia and Cryptosporidium.
Stomach pain, headache, nausea, yellow urine.
albendazole: Roundworm, hookworm, threadworm, tapeworm and other worms.
Blocks the worm's food uptake and kills it.
ivermectin: Scabies, lice and some worm infections.
Paralyses the parasite's nerves and muscles.
Take on an empty stomach with water, at the prescribed dose.
metronidazole: Amoebic dysentery, giardia, dental and abdominal infections, vaginal infections.
Damages the DNA of the germs.
No alcohol during the course and for 48 hours after.
amoxicillin: Bacterial infections of ear, throat, chest, urine and teeth.
Stops bacteria building their cell wall.
Not if allergic to penicillin. Finish the full course.
clavulanic: Combined with amoxicillin or cefuroxime to work against resistant bacteria.
Blocks the bacterial enzyme that destroys the antibiotic.
Taking at the start of a meal reduces stomach upset.
flucloxacillin: Skin and soft-tissue infections, boils, wound infections (staph).
Stops bacteria building their cell wall.
Take on an empty stomach. Not in penicillin allergy.
cephradine: Chest, urine, skin and soft-tissue infections.
Stops bacteria building their cell wall.
Tell your doctor about serious cephalosporin or penicillin allergy.
cefixime: Typhoid, urine infections, throat, ear and chest infections, gonorrhoea.
Stops bacteria building their cell wall.
Finish the full course. See a doctor for severe diarrhoea.
cefuroxime: Throat, sinus, ear, lung, urine and skin infections; Lyme disease.
Stops bacteria building their cell wall.
Better absorbed with food. Finish the full course.
cefpodoxime: Chest, throat, urine and skin infections.
Stops bacteria building their cell wall.
Take with food; finish the full course.
ceftriaxone: Serious infections: pneumonia, meningitis, typhoid, blood infection, surgical prophylaxis.
Stops bacteria building their cell wall.
Not given in the same line with calcium-containing fluids; under medical supervision.
ceftazidime: Stops bacteria building their cell wall.
cefepime: Pneumonia, serious urine and abdominal infections.
Stops bacteria building their cell wall.
meropenem: Very serious and multidrug-resistant hospital infections.
Stops bacteria building their cell wall.
Only under medical supervision; misuse drives resistance.
azithromycin: Throat, sinus, lung and skin infections, typhoid, some sexually transmitted infections.
Caution in irregular heartbeat. Usually a 3–5 day course.
clarithromycin: Chest and skin infections, H. pylori treatment.
Interacts with many medicines; tell your doctor everything you take.
ciprofloxacin: Urine infections, typhoid, diarrhoea, bone and joint infections; eye/ear drops.
Nausea, diarrhoea, dizziness; sometimes tendon pain.
Usually not for children or pregnancy. Do not take together with milk, antacids, iron or calcium.
levofloxacin: Pneumonia, sinus, urine and prostate infections.
Risk of tendon rupture (especially elderly). Not together with antacids or iron.
moxifloxacin: Pneumonia, sinus and skin infections; eye drops for eye infections.
doxycycline: Acne, chest infections, leptospirosis, some sexually transmitted infections.
Take upright with plenty of water. Not under 8 years or in pregnancy.
clindamycin: Skin, bone and dental infections; acne gel.
See a doctor immediately for severe or bloody diarrhoea.
linezolid: Serious infections with resistant germs (MRSA, VRE).
Blocks the very first step of bacterial protein making.
Long use can lower blood counts; not with some antidepressants.
cotrimoxazole: Urine infections, some diarrhoeas and lung infections.
Blocks bacterial folic acid production in two steps.
Nausea, rash; rarely severe skin reactions.
Not in sulfa allergy. Stop and see a doctor if a rash appears.
chloramphenicol: Do not touch the dropper tip to the eye.
neomycin: Wounds, burns and bacterial skin infections.
Not for long on large wounds; not in the ear with a perforated eardrum.
tobramycin: Do not use longer than directed.
fluconazole: Vaginal and oral thrush, skin and nail fungus.
Stops the fungus building its cell membrane.
Many drug interactions; caution in liver disease.
itraconazole: Ringworm, nail fungus, pityriasis and other fungal infections.
Stops the fungus building its cell membrane.
Not in heart failure; take after food.
voriconazole: Stops the fungus building its cell membrane.
terbinafine: Ringworm, nail and toe fungal infections.
Blocks production of a fungal membrane component.
Tablets not for people with liver disease.
ketoconazole: Dandruff, seborrhoeic dermatitis, ringworm and skin fungus.
Stops the fungus building its cell membrane.
Tablets can harm the liver; not without medical advice.
clotrimazole: Ringworm, fungal itch, vaginal thrush, nappy rash.
Keep applying for the full time even after symptoms go.
nystatin: Thrush of the mouth and food pipe.
Makes holes in the fungal membrane.
Hold in the mouth for a while before swallowing.
acyclovir: Stops the virus copying its DNA.
Drink plenty of water; dose reduced in kidney disease.
metformin: Reduces glucose made by the liver and improves insulin action.
Nausea, diarrhoea, stomach upset, metallic taste.
Take with food. Not in severe kidney disease; tell your doctor before contrast X-rays.
gliclazide: Increases insulin release from the pancreas.
Do not skip meals. Learn hypo signs (sweating, shaking).
glimepiride: Increases insulin release from the pancreas.
Low blood sugar, weight gain, dizziness.
Take with breakfast; skipping meals risks hypos.
sitagliptin: Type 2 diabetes, alone or with metformin.
Keeps incretin hormones that raise insulin after meals active longer.
Stop and see a doctor for severe stomach pain.
empagliflozin: Type 2 diabetes; also protects in heart failure and kidney disease.
Removes extra glucose through the urine.
Passing more urine, genital fungal infection, dehydration.
Drink enough water; seek advice when ill or fasting.
semaglutide: Raises insulin, lowers appetite and slows stomach emptying.
Not with family history of thyroid cancer or pancreatitis; under medical supervision.
insulin: Helps glucose enter cells, lowering blood sugar.
Low blood sugar, skin changes at injection site.
Dose and timing as directed; store in the fridge (do not freeze).
amlodipine: High blood pressure and chest pain (angina).
Widens blood vessels to lower pressure.
Do not stop suddenly; check blood pressure regularly.
losartan: High blood pressure, heart failure, kidney protection in diabetes.
Blocks angiotensin II, a hormone that narrows vessels.
Never in pregnancy. Kidney and potassium tests may be needed.
ramipril: High blood pressure, heart failure, protection after heart attack.
Reduces angiotensin production so vessels widen.
Not in pregnancy. Seek urgent care if face or lips swell.
bisoprolol: High blood pressure, angina, heart failure, fast heartbeat.
Slows the heart and reduces its workload.
Tiredness, cold hands and feet, slow pulse.
Do not stop suddenly. Tell your doctor if you have asthma.
hydrochlorothiazide: High blood pressure and fluid retention.
Removes salt and water through the kidneys to lower pressure.
More urine, low potassium, raised sugar and uric acid.
Take in the morning; salt and potassium tests may be needed.
furosemide: Fluid build-up in heart failure, kidney or liver disease.
Removes large amounts of salt and water through the kidneys.
More urine, dehydration, low potassium, dizziness.
Take in the morning; electrolytes need checking.
spironolactone: Heart failure, fluid in liver cirrhosis, some hormonal conditions.
Blocks aldosterone to remove salt and water.
High potassium, breast swelling or tenderness.
Not with potassium supplements; caution in kidney disease.
sacubitril: Boosts protective natural peptides and blocks angiotensin.
Low blood pressure, high potassium, dizziness.
Not with ACE inhibitors; not in pregnancy.
atorvastatin: High cholesterol; prevention of heart attack and stroke.
Reduces cholesterol production in the liver.
Report unexplained muscle pain or weakness. Not in pregnancy.
ezetimibe: High cholesterol, usually with a statin.
Reduces cholesterol absorption from the gut.
clopidogrel: Prevents clots after heart attack, stroke and stent placement.
Tell your doctor before surgery or tooth extraction; do not stop on your own.
enoxaparin: Prevention and treatment of vein clots (DVT), some heart conditions.
Inactivates clotting factors in the blood.
Under medical supervision; report any bleeding.
tranexamic: Heavy periods, surgery, nosebleeds and trauma bleeding.
Prevents blood clots from breaking down.
Not with a history of blood clots.
montelukast: Asthma prevention, allergic rhinitis, exercise-induced breathlessness.
Blocks leukotrienes that inflame the airways.
Headache, stomach pain; sometimes sleep or mood changes.
Not for sudden severe breathlessness. Report mood changes to your doctor.
doxophylline: Relaxes airway muscles to ease breathing.
Caution in heart disease and seizures.
salbutamol: Sudden breathlessness in asthma and COPD.
Needing it more than a few times a week means asthma is not controlled; see a doctor.
salmeterol: Control of asthma and COPD, usually with a steroid inhaler.
Keeps airway muscles relaxed for a long time.
Not for sudden attacks; never use alone in asthma.
fluticasone: Asthma prevention, COPD, allergic rhinitis and nasal polyps.
Reduces inflammation in the airways or nose.
Hoarse voice, oral thrush, dry nose.
Rinse your mouth after the inhaler. Use regularly.
ambroxol: Thins mucus so it is easier to cough up.
dextromethorphan: Calms the cough centre in the brain.
Not for chesty cough; ask a doctor for children.
fexofenadine: Allergic rhinitis, sneezing, itchy nose/eyes, itching and hives.
Blocks the action of histamine, the allergy chemical.
Headache, dry mouth; mild drowsiness with some.
Check whether it makes you drowsy before driving.
chlorpheniramine: Blocks histamine; also acts on the brain.
Avoid driving and alcohol; ask a doctor for young children.
ketotifen: Allergic rhinitis, eye allergy, add-on asthma prevention in children.
Stabilises mast cells and blocks histamine.
Full effect may take several weeks.
prednisolone: Asthma, severe allergy, arthritis and autoimmune disease, skin inflammation (creams), some cancers.
Increased appetite and weight, raised blood sugar, mood changes; bone loss with long use.
Do not stop suddenly after long use; taper. Do not use skin creams on the face for long.
clobetasol: Psoriasis, eczema and inflammation not helped by weaker steroids.
Not on face, groin or armpits; usually not over 2 weeks. Do not use on fungal infections.
clonazepam: Boosts GABA, the brain's calming chemical.
Habit-forming. Do not stop suddenly; avoid alcohol and driving. Prescription only.
flupentixol: Mild to moderate depression and anxiety.
Alters dopamine, serotonin and noradrenaline balance in the brain.
Ask your doctor before long-term use.
escitalopram: Increases serotonin levels in the brain.
Nausea, sleep changes, sweating, sexual problems.
Full effect takes 2–4 weeks. Do not stop suddenly; seek help at once for suicidal thoughts.
mirtazapine: Depression, especially with insomnia and poor appetite.
Increases noradrenaline and serotonin in the brain.
Take at night; do not stop suddenly.
quetiapine: Schizophrenia, bipolar disorder; sometimes add-on for depression.
Acts on dopamine and serotonin receptors in the brain.
Drowsiness, weight gain, raised sugar and lipids.
Under regular medical supervision; do not stop suddenly.
levetiracetam: Epilepsy; some also for bipolar disorder and migraine prevention.
Reduces abnormal electrical signals in the brain.
Stopping suddenly can trigger seizures. Valproate harms the baby in pregnancy.
flunarizine: Reduces calcium entry into brain vessels and nerve cells.
Not with a history of depression or Parkinson's.
levodopa: Replaces dopamine in the brain; carbidopa helps it reach the brain.
High-protein meals reduce absorption; do not stop suddenly.
trihexyphenidyl: Parkinson's disease and antipsychotic-induced muscle problems.
Dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, confusion.
sildenafil: Erectile dysfunction; tadalafil also for enlarged prostate and lung hypertension.
Widens blood vessels to increase blood flow locally.
Never with nitrate medicines for chest pain.
tamsulosin: Urinary problems from enlarged prostate; sometimes to pass kidney stones.
Relaxes muscles of the prostate and bladder neck.
Tell your eye surgeon before cataract surgery.
calcium: Calcium deficiency, osteoporosis, pregnancy and breastfeeding.
Supplies the main building block of bones and teeth.
Not at the same time as iron or thyroid medicines; caution with kidney stones.
vitamind: Vitamin D deficiency, prevention of bone loss and rickets; with calcium.
Increases calcium absorption from the gut.
High doses can raise blood calcium; take high doses only on medical advice.
vitaminb: Vitamin B deficiency, nerve weakness and tingling, mouth ulcers.
Supports nerves, blood formation and energy production.
Generally safe; urine may turn bright yellow.
Long-term high-dose B6 can damage nerves.
vitaminc: Vitamin C deficiency (scurvy), wound healing, helps iron absorption.
Acts as an antioxidant and is needed for collagen.
Stomach upset or diarrhoea at high doses.
Avoid high doses with a history of kidney stones.
vitamine: Avoid high doses with blood thinners.
zinc: Supports immunity and repair of the gut lining.
Take after food if it causes nausea.
iron: Not with tea, milk or calcium; keep out of children's reach.
folic: Prevents neural tube defects in pregnancy; folate-deficiency anaemia.
Needed to make new cells and blood.
Best started when planning pregnancy; check B12 first if deficient.
multivitamin: Covers dietary vitamin/mineral gaps, weakness after illness.
Supplies several vitamins and minerals together.
Not a substitute for a balanced diet; stacking supplements can overdose.
glucosamine: Thought to supply building blocks of cartilage.
Check the label if allergic to shellfish; takes weeks to work.
coq10: Supportive supplement in heart disease and statin muscle aches.
Takes part in cellular energy production.
May alter the effect of blood thinners.
povidone: Wound cleaning, skin disinfection before surgery, mouthwash.
Do not swallow; not for long on large burns or deep wounds.
lidocaine: Minor surgery, dental work, numbing painful areas (gel/spray).
Temporarily blocks pain signals in nerves.
Do not use large amounts or on large areas of broken skin.
oxymetazoline: Blocked nose from cold and sinusitis.
Narrows nasal blood vessels to reduce swelling.
Not more than 5–7 days in a row, or blockage gets worse.
timolol: Reduces eye fluid production or increases drainage.
Timolol needs caution in asthma and slow heartbeat.
menthol: Muscle and joint pain balms; salicylic acid for dandruff, acne and thick skin.
Gives a cooling/warming feeling that masks pain, or removes dead skin.
Do not apply to wounds or eyes.
dextrose: Dehydration, sugar and salt replacement, giving drugs into a vein.
Pain or swelling at the vein.

ors: Replaces water and salts in diarrhoea, vomiting, cholera and heat dehydration.
